idiom_name: public non-virtual entry point + protected virtual/abstract hook (the Dispose(bool) shape)
implementation_notes: C# members are non-virtual unless marked virtual or abstract, so the entry point is already non-overridable; the work is moving the customizable step into a protected virtual (or protected abstract) hook that the wrapper calls. The BCL's own template is IDisposable: a public, non-virtual Dispose() calls protected virtual Dispose(bool), and the Framework Design Guidelines state the rule directly - do not make the parameterless Dispose virtual, Dispose(bool) is the override point. Where a hierarchy must stay closed, seal the wrapper (`public sealed` / `sealed override`) so no further derived class can re-open it.
pitfalls: Marking the entry point `virtual` compiles fine and re-opens the contract - mirror the BCL rule that the public template method must not be virtual.
A protected abstract hook is a source-breaking change for existing subclasses; prefer a protected virtual hook with a default when third parties may derive from the type.
`protected internal` widens the hook to the whole assembly; use plain `protected` (or `private protected`) unless assembly-wide implementation is intended.
